column3: Names the One who created the speaker as the sole source of guidance, directly echoing the focus's Creator-grounded devotion.
Condemns worship of false authority, clarifying the rival worship that the focus rejects by implication.
Grounds lordship in the Creator of heavens and earth, closely paralleling the focus's reason for worship.
Concludes the surah with universal dominion and return to God, directly completing the focus's final claim.
The oath by the wise Quran does not clarify worship, creation, or return.
Affirms that all affairs return to God, reinforcing the focus's final destination.
States categorical refusal to worship what others worship, sharpening the focus's exclusive devotion.
Identifies the messenger whose warning sets the immediate narrative in which the focus speaks.
Pairs separation from false worship with worship of God alone, a practical parallel to the focus's allegiance.
Names the One who created the speaker as the basis of his independent prophetic stance.
Reception of revelation and testimony do not materially clarify the focus's worship-creation-return sequence.
Commands worship of God alone, directly supporting the focus's exclusive worship claim.
Combines God's exclusive deity, judgment, and return to Him, closely matching the focus's authority horizon.
The warning's ineffectiveness does not clarify the speaker's reason for worship.
Connects death directly to return to the Lord, specifying the return asserted in the focus.
Denies that the addressees worship what the speaker worships, making exclusive devotion a stable distinction.
The image of barriers to sight does not clarify worship, creation, or return.
Confesses belonging to God and returning to Him, giving the focus's return a personal expression.
The search for the hoopoe uses neither creation nor final return in the focus's sense.
God's taking and releasing souls offers a limited death-horizon for the focus's return.
Joins worshippers to what they worship, clarifying the relational object of the focus's worship question.
Rejects any other deity and ends with judgment and return to God, a close parallel to the focus.
The receptive audience's reward does not directly clarify the focus's declaration.
Its description of the sky splitting shares the creation root but not the focus's Creator or return argument.
Rejects worship of those invoked besides God and links that refusal to guidance.
The threat of drowning and lack of rescue do not clarify worship, creation, or return.
Pharaoh's arrogance includes denying return to God, providing a contrary stance to the focus.
Rejects idol worship, commands worship and gratitude to God, and ends with return to Him.
The sale of Joseph does not materially clarify the focus's themes.
Commands believers to worship God alone despite changes of place, reinforcing exclusive devotion.
Unites universal ownership, the Hour, and return to God under one sovereign authority.
Introduces the town-and-messengers scene in which the focus's speaker enters and declares faith.
Its standing before the Lord gives only a limited judgment context; its return is reciprocal speech among people.
Combines worship of God without association, calling to Him, and return to Him in one declaration.
Temporary mercy and enjoyment do not clarify the focus's worship or final return.
Exposes a false object of worship as unable to answer, harm, or benefit, contrasting it with the focus's Creator.
Directs the whole person to the Creator of heavens and earth while rejecting association.
The reference to the clear Book does not clarify the focus's argument.
Commands worship and fear of God, directly reinforcing the focus's chosen allegiance.
Commands worship of the Lord who owns all things, supplying a clear sovereignty basis for worship.
Continues the messenger narrative whose rejection elicits the focus's testimony.
Its inability to move forward or back uses return in an unrelated physical sense.
Assigns judgment to God and describes turning to Him, reinforcing His exclusive final authority.
Garden provision does not clarify worship, creation, or return.
Explicitly states that jinn and humankind were created for God's worship, joining creation to worship.
The isolated reference to unseen things provides no material clarification.
Declares religion sincere for God alone and rejects worship of intermediaries.
Directly affirms God's power to return the human being, supporting the focus's return claim.
Moses's request for ease does not clarify the focus's themes.
Records the town's rejection of divine sending, the immediate opposition to the focus's witness.
Calling Khidr a servant of God gives only a general resonance with worship.
Its presumptuous mention of return to the Lord gives a limited contrast to accountable return.
Commands worship of God and identifies it as the straight path in the same surah.
Rejects family pressure toward association and grounds the refusal in return to God and disclosure of deeds.
Thanksgiving for offspring and answered prayer do not clarify the focus's sequence.
Links rejection or gratitude to personal responsibility and final return to the Lord.
Combines giving life, causing death, and return to God in one divine sequence.
Creation's ordered heavens support divine creative power, but its command to look again is unrelated to final return.
Continues the messengers' testimony within the immediate scene that the focus answers.
States that all matters return to God, reinforcing the focus's final direction.
The splitting sky shares only the creation-root language, not the focus's argument.
The straight path alone does not clarify the worship-creation-return relation.
Anticipated meeting with the Lord and return to Him make the focus's final claim personally accountable.
At final judgment Satan disowns the association people gave him, exposing misplaced allegiance.
The recording of speech and extended punishment do not directly clarify the focus's themes.
Names God as Creator of heavens and earth while confronting inherited worship, closely supporting the focus.
God's sole divinity, living self-subsistence, and ownership of all creation support the focus's worship rationale.
States the messengers' duty of clear delivery in the immediate narrative context.
Places final decision within the certainty that all affairs return to God.
Explicitly joins initial creation, restoration, and return to God, directly deepening the focus's creation-return logic.
God's creation of livestock gives a limited same-surah sign of creative ownership.
Marital reconciliation uses return in a legal sense unrelated to final return.
Declares worship of God alone with sincere religion, directly paralleling the focus's exclusive devotion.
The legal penalties for violent corruption do not clarify worship, creation, or return.
God's inheritance of earth and its people culminates in their return to Him.
Restricts prayer to the Lord and rejects associating anyone with Him.
Shows the hostile response to the messengers that frames the focus's intervening declaration.
God's control of provision for His servants offers only a broad sovereignty resonance.
Rejects worship of others and worships God who causes death, grounding exclusive devotion in ultimate authority.
The creation of additional vessels does not materially clarify the focus's argument.
Sets out life, death, renewed life, and return to God as a complete human trajectory.
Seals the reciprocal denial of worship, making distinct objects of devotion permanent.
The preservation of a believer's righteous effort gives only a distant accountability context.
Return to Hell supplies a particular terminal outcome but does not clarify the focus's Creator-grounded worship.
Names God as Lord and Creator of everything while denying any other deity.
The messengers reject the town's superstition and name its excess, immediately preparing the focus's correction.
Describes Noah as one of God's believing servants, only broadly resonating with worship.
Names God as Lord and states that people return to Him, reinforcing the focus's final authority.
God's command over a historical victory does not clarify worship, creation, or return.
States return to God followed by full recompense for every soul, clarifying the focus's accountable return.
The speaker's lack of power over harm or guidance does not clarify the focus's themes.
At the gathering God confronts alleged worship objects with their worshippers, exposing false devotion.
Entry among God's servants offers only a general resonance with worship.
States that every soul tastes death and then returns to God, directly specifying the focus's final movement.
Undercuts alleged partners as conjectural, supporting the focus's exclusive worship stance.
Rejects association despite parental pressure and ends with return to God for disclosure of deeds.
God's knowledge of His servants is a broad sovereignty resonance without the focus's sequence.
Answers restoration by appealing to the One who created people the first time.
Contrasts willing worship of God with arrogant refusal and ends with universal gathering to Him.
Condemns worship of powerless beings besides God, directly contrasting the focus's Creator-directed worship.
The believing man enters the same scene by urging his people to follow the messengers, immediately leading into the focus's confession.
His call to follow unpaid and rightly guided messengers is the direct premise for the focus's question about worship.
The next verse rejects taking lesser gods whose intercession cannot help, directly completing the focus's exclusive worship argument.
It states that choosing such gods would be manifest error, the immediate consequence of abandoning the focus's worship.
The speaker declares faith in the people's Lord, resolving the confession begun in the focus.
The command to enter Paradise supplies the immediate outcome of the speaker's faithful worship and witness.
The speaker attributes forgiveness and honor to his Lord, completing the local witness-and-reward sequence.
Commands worship of the Lord who created the audience and those before them, directly joining worship to creation.
States that God resurrects the dead and that they return to Him, directly clarifying the focus's final movement.
Names God as Creator of all things and explicitly commands worship of Him.
Commands sincere devotion to God and pairs human origination with return to Him.
Names the Creator and then asks who should be worshipped besides Him, closely matching the focus's reasoning.
Combines universal return, God's originating and restoring creation, and recompense.
Identifies God as the One who begins creation and restores it, excluding rivals from that authority.
States that judgment belongs to God and that He commanded worship of none but Him.
Contrasts the Creator with one who cannot create, strengthening the focus's reason for directing worship to the Creator.
Gives the universal prophetic command to worship God and avoid false authorities.
Records the objection to being raised as a new creation after death, directly framing the focus's return horizon.
Answers resurrection denial by affirming renewed creation after people become bones and dust.
States the challenge of being brought forth alive after death, directly engaging the focus's return implication.
Answers that challenge by recalling God's first creation of the person from nothing.
Defines every messenger's proclamation as worship of God alone.
Makes the first creation the model for the promised restoration of creation.
Uses human origination and the revival of dead earth as signs establishing resurrection.
Explicitly affirms the Hour and God's raising of those in graves.
Combines God's giving life, causing death, and giving life again.
Commands believers to bow, prostrate, and worship their Lord, directly reinforcing the focus's devotion.
States that people die after their created earthly life, supplying the first stage of the focus's return horizon.
States that people will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.
Rejects purposeless creation and affirms that people return to God.
Condemns invoking another god without proof, clarifying the false worship the focus excludes.
Explicitly asks who begins creation and restores it, then exposes the incoherence of associating partners with God.
States that God begins creation and restores it, a direct parallel to the focus's Creator-and-return logic.
Calls people to observe how creation began and then affirms God's final creation.
States that God begins creation and restores it, directly supporting return after first creation.
Places creation, provision, death, and renewed life under God's exclusive power.
Uses revived dead earth as an explicit analogy for God's resurrection of the dead.
Declares that creating and resurrecting all humanity is like doing so for one soul.
Asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, grounding exclusive devotion in creative sovereignty.
Explicitly compares God's reviving dead land to His raising of the dead.
Shows that alleged partners cannot hear or answer invocation and will deny their association.
States the challenge of who will give life to decayed bones, directly developing the focus's return implication.
Answers that the One who created bones the first time will give them life again.
Argues that the Creator of heavens and earth can create people anew.
States that God's command brings about whatever He wills, completing the local resurrection argument.
Acknowledges God as Creator of heavens and earth while exposing the inconsistency of invoking others.
Names God as Creator of all things and guardian over them.
Depicts death at the trumpet blast followed by people rising, making return concrete.
Describes God as the maker of heavens, earth, and human form, supporting His creative authority.
Commands sincere invocation of the living God who alone is deity.
Appeals to first creation and states that people return to God in a judgment scene.
Records the admission that God created them, exposing the contradiction of turning away from Him.
Challenges people to recognize God, rather than themselves, as the creator of human life.
Names God as the One who created people, spread them, and will gather them to Himself.
